GPT-Style Language Models

Understanding large models from scratch

Next-word prediction — tokens — neural networks — attention — training — generation — chat assistants
slides.title: GPT-Style Language Models

slides.html:
What this deck will give you

  • A clear picture of what ChatGPT-like models actually do
  • How text becomes numbers and flows through the model
  • How the model learns, and what training costs
  • Why it talks nonsense with total confidence at times

No background needed: high-school math is enough; matrices, probability and gradients come with small numeric examples.
slides.title: What this deck will give you

slides.html: 0. What Does a Large Model Do?
slides.title: 0. What Does a Large Model Do?

slides.html:
Start from phone autocomplete

Type "The weather today is" and the keyboard suggests: nice / hot / cold

  • That is a tiny language model: guess the next word from what precedes it
  • ChatGPT does the same thing: it has read far more and has a far bigger "brain"
  • Guess a word → append it → guess again → a whole passage appears

A "super word-chain champion" who read the whole internet: to continue convincingly it must learn grammar, common sense, facts and reasoning.
slides.title: Start from phone autocomplete

slides.html:
Three sentences

  1. A language model is a fill-in-the-blank function: preceding text → probabilities of the next word
  2. Training: fill blanks over huge text, check answers, improve
  3. Chat assistant = fill-in champion + a little extra coaching (demonstrations and scoring)
slides.title: Three sentences

slides.html:
A sense of scale

  • GPT-2 (1.6B parameters): about US$43,000 at the time
  • Now: about 1.4B parameters, 8 H100s, 1.65–3 hours, under US$100
  • Total compute about 3–4\times10^{19} operations
  • The resulting assistant is "like a kindergartener": short stories, but often makes things up
slides.title: A sense of scale

slides.html: 1. The Language Model: Predicting the Next Word
slides.title: 1. The Language Model: Predicting the Next Word
The output is a probability list

slides.html:
A sentence's probability = product of word probabilities

p(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{t}p(x_t\mid x_{<t})

"I love you": 0.02\times0.05\times0.3=0.0003

One word at a time, left to right: autoregressive.
slides.title: A sentence's probability = product of word probabilities

slides.html:
How to measure "good": the loss

\text{loss}=-\ln p(\text{the true next word})
Probability given to the truth 0.99 0.5 0.1 0.01
Loss 0.01 0.69 2.30 4.61
  • Accurate prediction → small loss; confidently wrong → heavy penalty
  • Training = making the average loss smaller and smaller
slides.title: How to measure "good": the loss

slides.html:
Why "just guessing the next word" teaches so much

  • "The capital of France is ___" → remember facts
  • "Keys on the table, then he left. The keys are on the ___" → common sense
  • "2 + 3 = ___" → calculation
  • Half-written code → syntax and logic

Nobody teaches the rules one by one; they are by-products of guessing well.
slides.title: Why "just guessing the next word" teaches so much

slides.html: 2. Turning Text into Numbers
slides.title: 2. Turning Text into Numbers

slides.html:
How finely to cut?

Cut Problem
Letters sequences too long, a letter means little
Whole words unbounded vocabulary, new words fail
Subwords (BPE) common words whole, rare words in parts
slides.title: How finely to cut?

slides.html:
BPE: repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair

Corpus: low(5) lower(2) newest(6) widest(3)

Step Most frequent pair Merged into
1 e+s (9) es
2 es+t (9) est
3 l+o (7) lo
4 lo+w (7) low

New word lowest → low + est: never seen, but we know the parts.
slides.title: BPE: repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair

slides.html:
The real vocabulary

  • Size V=2^{15}=32768, including 9 special tokens
  • <|bos|>, user/assistant start and end, python/output markers
  • Numbers grouped 1–2 digits at a time
  • Starts from 256 bytes: any text can be represented
slides.title: The real vocabulary

slides.html: 3. Neural Networks and Training
slides.title: 3. Neural Networks and Training

slides.html:
Building blocks: weighted sum + nonlinearity

Wx,\ \ \max(0,z),\ \ \mathrm{softmax}
  • Matrix multiplication = many weighted sums; weights = knobs (parameters)
  • ReLU: negatives become 0; lets the network express complex patterns
  • softmax: any scores → probabilities summing to 1

(2.0,1.0,0.1)\ \to\ (0.66,0.24,0.10)
slides.title: Building blocks: weighted sum + nonlinearity

slides.html: 4. The Transformer and Attention
slides.title: 4. The Transformer and Attention

slides.html:
A small example

q=(1,0), three words with keys/values:

Word k v Weight
1 (1,0) (10,0) 0.40
2 (0,1) (0,10) 0.20
3 (1,1) (5,5) 0.40

Output =0.4(10,0)+0.2(0,10)+0.4(5,5)=(6,4)

\mathrm{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt d}\Big)V
slides.title: A small example

slides.html:
Causal mask, heads and position

  • Causal mask: see only yourself and earlier words; no peeking at the answer
  • Multiple heads: several viewpoints in parallel (reference, neighbours, syntax...)
  • Position encoding: otherwise "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look the same
slides.title: Causal mask, heads and position

slides.html:
MLP and residuals

  • Attention = "a meeting"; MLP = "back at your desk, thinking"
  • Residual connection: add a small change to the original vector, like annotating a draft
  • About 12d^2 parameters per layer (attention 4d^2 + MLP 8d^2)

Model size is set by two knobs: width d and depth L.
slides.title: MLP and residuals

slides.html: 5. Training a Real Model
slides.title: 5. Training a Real Model

slides.html:
Data: quality beats quantity

Experiment Result
Switch to a better corpus time -27\%
Unfiltered web text score 0.2602 → 0.2241
Other "bigger, newer" mixtures all worse

Do not assume; test against a fixed metric.
slides.title: Data: quality beats quantity
Scaling laws: bigger is better, with diminishing returns

slides.html: 6. Generation and Inference
slides.title: 6. Generation and Inference

slides.html:
Why it "makes things up"

  • The model learns "what sounds like something a person says", not "what is true"
  • When unsure, it continues with "something shaped like an answer"
  • Plausible \neq true

Check important facts; let the model use tools.
slides.title: Why it "makes things up"
The KV cache: do not reread everything

slides.html:
Using tools

  1. The model writes <|python_start|> expression <|python_end|>
  2. The system computes it with a restricted calculator
  3. The result is forced back into the context
  4. The model keeps writing and quotes it

Good at plausible continuation, poor at exact arithmetic: hand it to a tool.
slides.title: Using tools

slides.title: 7. From Continuation to Assistant
SFT: learn from demonstrations, loss on the assistant only

slides.html: 8. Review
slides.title: 8. Review

slides.html:
One-page summary

  1. A language model assigns probabilities to the next word; loss =-\ln p
  2. Text → tokens → word vectors
  3. Transformer = L blocks of (attention + MLP) with residuals
  4. Training = guess, compare, adjust (gradient descent + backpropagation)
  5. Scale: C\approx6ND, the loss falls slowly as a power law
  6. Generation = sampling word by word; temperature, KV cache, tools
  7. Assistant = pretraining + SFT + RL
  8. Limit: only learns "plausible continuation", so it makes things up
slides.title: One-page summary

slides.html:
Common misconceptions

Misconception Correct
The model "looks up" the internet It stores only statistics in its parameters
It "understands" like a person Ability is a by-product of learning plausible continuation
Always taking the top word is best Repetitive and stiff; sample instead
Per-token loss compares vocabularies Use bpb
SFT loss on the whole conversation Only on the assistant's words
Decoding is compute bound It is bandwidth bound
slides.title: Common misconceptions
